short: Seven Ming fleets crossed the Indian Ocean, then the programme was cancelled outright.
full:
Zheng He was a Muslim from Yunnan, taken captive as a boy, castrated and raised in the household of the future Yongle Emperor. From 1405 he commanded seven expeditions that reached Java, Sumatra, Ceylon, Calicut, Hormuz, Aden and the Swahili coast at Mogadishu and Malindi. The fleets carried some 27,000 men in over two hundred vessels, including the largest wooden ships built anywhere to that date. They were not voyages of discovery: the routes were long established by Arab and Malay traders, and the purpose was to enrol distant rulers in the Ming tribute system.

Force was used when required — a pirate fleet destroyed at Palembang, a Sinhalese king carried back to Nanjing in 1411 — and exotic tribute came home, including a giraffe presented in 1414 as an auspicious qilin. Zheng He died during or just after the seventh voyage in 1433. Officials had long argued the fleets were an extravagance with no return, and the court ended the programme; within decades ocean-going shipbuilding on that scale had been abandoned.
